blocks.label: Overview
blocks.text: You’ll learn in sequence, from the idea of using resources as needed to responsibility boundaries and designs that prepare for failures.

blocks.label: Learning objectives
blocks.text: Distinguish usage levels, the layers you are responsible for, and the scope of failures, and explain why you would choose a particular cloud configuration.

blocks.label: Learning objectives
blocks.text: Explain why to adjust usage based on on-demand pricing and pay-as-you-go billing.

blocks.label: Determine which responsibilities belong to AWS and the user based on the service used and the layer being managed.
blocks.text: Explain the Region/AZ hierarchy and shared failure domains.

blocks.label: Learning objectives…1 more step
blocks.text: Based on on-demand pricing and pay-as-you-go billing, explain why to adjust usage.

steps.label: Based on the service used and the layer being managed, determine which responsibilities belong to AWS and the user.

blocks.label: Learning objectives
blocks.text: Compare architectures by distinguishing load, failures, and costs.

blocks.label: Provision resources when needed and adjust capacity
blocks.text: To run an application, you need servers for computing, a place to store data, and a network for communication. If you buy the equipment yourself, you decide how many units you need and where to install them before use begins. If you have too little, you must wait for more equipment to be procured; if you have too much, you pay for equipment that goes unused.

blocks.label: In the cloud, you can provision these kinds of resources over a network as needed. On demand means requesting and using resources when you need them. Instead of buying enough from the start to handle the busiest periods, you can start small and adjust capacity based on usage.
blocks.text: Provision resources when needed and adjust capacity

steps.label: Provision resources when needed and adjust capacity

blocks.label: Provision when needed and right-size as needs change
blocks.text: Scaling out means increasing the number of instances that share the workload; scaling in means reducing that number. Scaling up means increasing the capacity of a single instance. The ability to change something is different from having it change automatically, so configure conditions and limits if you want automatic scaling.

blocks.label: With pay-as-you-go pricing, factors such as usage time, stored data volume, and number of operations affect costs. Stopping compute resources you no longer use does not necessarily eliminate charges for disks or stored data you keep. Check each resource to see what is in use and what remains.
blocks.text: Provision when needed and right-size as needs change

steps.label: Provision when needed and right-size as needs change

blocks.label: Scenario
blocks.text: We’re moving an internal reporting workload to the cloud. It runs at a small scale on weekdays, with usage increasing only at the end of each month.

blocks.label: Step 1
blocks.text: Measure weekday demand and avoid running enough capacity for the end-of-month peak all the time.

blocks.label: Step 2
blocks.text: Scale up computing resources to handle the end-of-month workload, then scale them back down afterward.

blocks.label: Step 3
blocks.text: Keep any data you still need after stopping compute, and check storage costs separately.

blocks.label: Conclusion
blocks.text: You can assess peak capacity needs and normal operating costs separately. Usage must be monitored and adjusted.

blocks.label: This is incorrect
blocks.text: Moving to the cloud always reduces costs without any effort.

blocks.label: Correction
blocks.text: Costs also rise when you run, store, or transfer more resources than necessary. Measure what you need, then review your design and usage.

steps.label: This is incorrect and its correction

blocks.label: Key takeaway
blocks.text: On-demand means resources are available when needed.

blocks.label: Consider the means of making changes separately from automation settings.
blocks.text: Review costs by usage factor, such as compute and storage.

blocks.label: What AWS manages and what you must protect
blocks.text: Using the cloud does not mean handing every security measure over to AWS. The shared responsibility model clarifies the boundary between the parts AWS manages and the parts customers manage.

blocks.label: What AWS manages and what you must protect
blocks.text: AWS manages the foundation that runs its services, including data center access and facilities. Customers, in turn, decide and configure who can access their data, what data to store, and how much network traffic to allow.

blocks.label: What AWS manages and what you must protect
blocks.text: The boundary varies by service. When you run an OS that you manage on EC2, you are responsible for updating that OS and the applications you install. With a service such as S3, where you do not directly operate an OS, AWS manages the underlying infrastructure, but you remain responsible for settings such as the scope of data access.

steps.label: What AWS manages and what you must protect

blocks.label: What AWS handles and what you protect yourself
blocks.text: To determine who is responsible, first check which service you are using, then identify the layer involved. Don’t lump everything together as “AWS’s responsibility because it’s on AWS” or “the customer’s responsibility because it involves data.” Instead, find out who configures and operates what for that resource.

steps.label: What AWS handles and what you protect yourself

blocks.label: Scenario
blocks.text: An update is needed for the OS of a web application running on EC2.

blocks.label: Step 1
blocks.text: Identify that the target is the guest OS managed by the customer, not the AWS physical server.

blocks.label: Step 2
blocks.text: The customer plans and applies the OS update, then verifies that it works.

blocks.label: Step 3
blocks.text: At the same time, also check whether there is any unnecessary network exposure or excessive application permissions.

blocks.label: Conclusion
blocks.text: Even when AWS protects the infrastructure, users still need to secure the OS and applications they manage.

blocks.label: This is incorrect
blocks.text: With a managed service, users no longer need to check security settings.

blocks.label: Correction
blocks.text: Even when more layers of operations are handled for you, responsibilities on the user side, such as data and access permissions, remain.

blocks.label: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Check the responsibility boundary for each service.

blocks.label: Distinguish the physical infrastructure from the customer’s configurations and data.
blocks.text: Customers are responsible for updating the guest OS on EC2 instances.

blocks.label: Key takeaway
blocks.text: AWS: Shared Responsibility Model

blocks.label: Separate failure domains with Regions and AZs
blocks.text: A Region is a geographic area where AWS resources are located. Choose one based on factors such as distance from users, the services you need, and constraints on where data can be stored. Simply switching the Region in the console does not move resources you have already created.

blocks.label: An Availability Zone (AZ) is an isolated location within a Region. An AZ consists of one or more data centers. It is important not to think of an AZ and a Region as locations of the same scale.
blocks.text: Putting two servers in the same AZ may help you prepare for the failure of one server. However, an issue affecting the entire AZ could make both servers unavailable. Distributing workloads across different AZs separates this shared failure domain.

blocks.label: Separate failure domains with Regions and AZs.
blocks.text: Separate failure domains with Regions and AZs.

steps.label: Separate failure domains with Regions and AZs.

blocks.label: Separating failure scopes with Regions and AZs
blocks.text: Placing resources in multiple AZs alone does not complete recovery for the entire system. Connections from users must be routed to processing destinations that are still available, and users must be able to access the data they need. Replication to another Region also requires configuration and operations for the relevant service; all data is not automatically replicated around the world.

steps.label: Separating failure scopes with Regions and AZs

blocks.label: Situation
blocks.text: We run a website on two servers in the same AZ and want to prepare for an AZ failure as well.

blocks.label: Step 1
blocks.text: Confirm that the two existing servers share the same failure domain: an AZ.

blocks.label: Step 2
blocks.text: Consider a setup that also runs workloads in a different AZ and routes traffic to a healthy destination.

blocks.label: Step 3
blocks.text: Check whether it can keep running with the remaining processing capacity and necessary data, even if one AZ becomes unavailable.

blocks.label: Conclusion
blocks.text: By looking beyond the number of instances to their placement and dependencies, you can explain which failures the architecture is designed to withstand.

blocks.label: This is incorrect
blocks.text: Increasing the number to two makes it possible to withstand an AZ failure, regardless of placement.

blocks.label: Correction
blocks.text: Two instances in the same AZ share the impact of an AZ failure. Check the number of instances and the failure scope separately.

steps.label: This is incorrect and the correction

blocks.label: Key takeaway
blocks.text: A Region contains multiple AZs.

blocks.label: Using multiple AZs helps limit the impact of a single-AZ failure.
blocks.text: Check communication and data dependencies, not just placement.

blocks.label: Key takeaway
blocks.text: AWS: Regions and Availability Zones

blocks.label: Design around why downtime matters and the budget available
blocks.text: Availability is the ability to use a service when it is needed. The same configuration is not suitable for every system. First, clarify who would be affected if it stopped, how long they can wait, and what kinds of failures the system needs to withstand.

blocks.label: For example, the impact of downtime differs between a temporary learning environment and a system that takes orders during business hours. For the latter, consider multiple processing targets and failover in the event of a failure. Also account for the added costs and management burden that come with more resources and operations.
blocks.text: Also distinguish increased load from failures. Adding processing capacity can make it easier to handle congestion, but if all the added resources are in the same failure domain, protection against an outage in that location is still inadequate. Adjusting capacity and distributing placement serve different purposes.

blocks.label: Design around why downtime matters and the budget available.
blocks.text: Design around why downtime matters and the budget available.

steps.label: Design around why downtime matters and the budget available.

blocks.label: Why You Can’t Stop Everything—and Designing Within Your Budget
blocks.text: When comparing designs, put into words what each one prevents, what risks remain, and whether you can operate it within that budget. Knowing the names of cloud features is not enough; understanding the risks that remain provides a foundation for choosing services in the next unit.

steps.label: Why You Can’t Stop Everything—and Designing Within Your Budget

blocks.label: Scenario
blocks.text: Compare two options. Option A has three instances in the same AZ; Option B has two instances in different AZs.

blocks.label: Step 1
blocks.text: Measure the required throughput instead of judging which option performs better based only on the number of instances.

blocks.label: Step 2
blocks.text: If the goal is to prepare for an AZ failure, check which shared failure modes Option B’s placement reduces.

blocks.label: Step 3
blocks.text: For option B as well, check the processing capacity of the one remaining instance, the connection switchover, and whether the required data can still be reached.

blocks.label: Conclusion
blocks.text: This lets you compare performance, the scope of failures, and operating costs separately instead of stopping at “more instances means safer.”

blocks.label: This is incorrect
blocks.text: Using multiple AZs means there is no need to consider load handling or check costs.

blocks.label: Correction
blocks.text: Distributing across AZs prepares for failure scenarios. Remaining capacity and costs should be checked separately.

blocks.label: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Consider the required availability in terms of the impact of an outage.

blocks.label: Do not confuse adjusting capacity with distributing the scope of failures.
blocks.text: Explain the remaining risks and operational burden, not just the benefits.

blocks.label: Key takeaway
blocks.text: AWS: Regions and Availability Zones
